clinicalPearls: SCA31 is an autosomal dominant, late-onset, pure cerebellar ataxia caused by an intronic pentanucleotide repeat insertion containing (TGGAA)n within a region shared by the BEAN1 and TK2 genes.
It is one of the commonest dominant ataxias in Japan, particularly among older adults, but is rare in most other populations.
Onset is characteristically late, often in or after later middle age, with slowly progressive gait ataxia, limb ataxia and dysarthria.
Sensorineural hearing impairment and reduced distal vibration sense are recognised additional features in some patients.
Horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus and other cerebellar eye signs are typical, whereas marked extracerebellar disease is unusual.
The disease-specific insertion carries (TGGAA)n repeats absent from normal chromosomes; it is this TGGAA element, not the benign flanking pentanucleotides, that is pathogenic.
MRI shows predominantly cerebellar, especially vermian, atrophy with relative brainstem sparing.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA31 is caused by a long, complex pentanucleotide repeat insertion — comprising (TGGAA)n together with (TAGAA)n, (TAAAA)n and mixed components — located in an intron shared, in opposite orientations, by BEAN1 (brain-expressed, associated with NEDD4, 1) and TK2 (thymidine kinase 2) on chromosome 16q. The disease-specific (TGGAA)n component is transcribed into RNA that forms nuclear RNA foci and sequesters RNA-binding and splicing proteins, and may undergo repeat-associated non-AUG translation into pentapeptide-repeat proteins; these gain-of-function RNA and protein toxicities preferentially damage cerebellar Purkinje cells. Normal individuals lack the TGGAA insertion, carrying only benign flanking pentanucleotide stretches, which is why the presence of the TGGAA element is diagnostic rather than a simple change in repeat length.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 (CACNA1A) — late-onset, slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia and a key mimic
SCA36 (NOP56) — late-onset ataxia that may include hearing loss and motor-neuron features
SCA15/16 (ITPR1) — very slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia
Sporadic late-onset cerebellar ataxia and the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy
Acquired ataxias in older adults, including alcohol-related, paraneoplastic and superficial siderosis
additionalInvestigations: Specialised insertion-specific or Southern-blot-based testing for the SCA31 TGGAA insertion, as standard repeat panels may not detect it
Exclusion of the common repeat-expansion ataxias, especially SCA6 in this age group
Brain MRI to document cerebellar atrophy
Pure-tone audiometry where hearing impairment is suspected
Nerve conduction and vibration testing where a sensory neuropathy is suspected
Family pedigree analysis and genetic counselling with cascade testing
redFlags: Rapid progression, prominent autonomic failure or early falls suggest the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy rather than SCA31.
Prominent motor-neuron features such as fasciculations and marked wasting point towards SCA36 or an alternative diagnosis.
Acute or subacute onset in an older adult mandates evaluation for an acquired cause.
reference.prognosis: SCA31 is slowly progressive and relatively benign; gait deteriorates gradually over many years but life expectancy is generally preserved, with walking aids needed only later.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because routine expansion panels do not include the specific SCA31 TGGAA insertion assay.
Ascribing late-onset ataxia in an older patient to ageing, alcohol or cerebrovascular disease without considering a dominant genetic cause.
Overlooking a family history obscured by late onset, with older affected relatives dying of unrelated causes.
Forgetting to look for associated sensorineural hearing loss.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so anchor care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Arrange audiological assessment and hearing aids for the associated sensorineural hearing impairment
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids, with attention to the reduced distal vibration sense
Monitor for bulbar dysfunction with periodic swallow assessment
Provide multidisciplinary ataxia clinic follow-up, reflecting the relatively benign, slowly progressive course
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing using insertion-specific assays for the TGGAA repeat
